newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Sihanouk watches from China as Cambodia erupts.
newsitem.headline: Sihanouk watches from China as Cambodia erupts.

text.p: Cambodia's King Norodom Sihanouk, who intervened from Beijing on Sunday to try to end factional fighting in his homeland, has personified the country's tragic misfortunes through five decades of war and peace.

Now 74 and ailing, he made a desperate plea to the feuding co-premiers, his son Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Vietnam's former protege Hun Sen, to end the fighting which rocked Phnom Penh at the weekend.
He summoned them to join him in the Chinese capital, where he is undergoing medical treatment, to negotiate a political settlement.

Sihanouk, a quixotic and colourful ruler, has seen the end of a long and bitter civil war, the country's first free and fair election and the establishment of a reconciliation government and restoration of the monarchy.

He played a pivotal role in winning these gains as the only figure able to command the respect of the world community and the four factions, including the radical Khmer Rouge guerrilla group, that agreed to peace in 1991 after 21 years of strife.

The king, setting the interests of the nation above personal distaste, agreed to a government request last September and signed a royal pardon for Ieng Sary for his role in the genocide of more than one million people as foreign minister during the 1975-79 Khmer Rouge rule.
The gesture by Sihanouk, a number of whose relatives died at Khmer Rouge hands, allowed a successful conclusion to peace talks between the government and the dissident leader.
His role as the promoter of peace and democracy and champion of human rights removed some of the tarnish left by his at times autocratic rule of the 1950s and 1960s.
Recently Sihanouk has become no more than a cipher, a king who reigns but does not rule, and has been powerless to prevent the eclipse of the royalists by his erstwhile socialist foes.

Sihanouk, the master manipulator and tactician, was ultimately outmanoeuvered by Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, and acknowledged this in April 1996, telling Le Monde that the premier was Cambodia's real strongman.

His judgement appeared to have been vindicated on Sunday, with reports from Phnom Penh indicating that Hun Sen's forces were tightening their grip on the capital after two days of heavy fighting with Ranariddh's troops.

Ironically, the king has come full circle since his first entry on to the political stage, when he was unexpectedly chosen by the French colonial government to succeed his uncle, Sisowath Monivong, on the throne in September 1941.
The French engineered his accession to the throne in the belief that he would be more pliable than the direct heir.
But Sihanouk took on the French and led an ultimately successful independence crusade, ending French rule in 1953.

The first 10 years in the life of modern Cambodia are now seen as a golden age, but also a time when Sihanouk was able to impose an iron rule over political foes. His master stroke of abdicating in 1955 enabled him to pursue political ambitions unfettered by royal constraints.
The honeymoon soured in the 1960s as Sihanouk came down heavily on opponents while struggling to keep his country out of the growing conflagration in neighbouring Vietnam.
He courted West and East but annoyed conservatives and corrupt elements in business circles by rejecting U.S. aid in 1963 and cutting ties with Washington in 1965.

His balancing act almost kept Cambodia out of the war, although Sihanouk allowed China to ship arms to the communist Vietnamese and in 1969 turned a blind eye when then U.S. president Richard Nixon ordered the bombing of communist bases in eastern Cambodia.
While on a trip to Moscow in 1970 Sihanouk was ousted in a U.S.-backed coup led by right-wing General Lon Nol.
Sihanouk fled to the jungle to join communist fighters he had once contemptuously dubbed "Les Khmers Rouges", an alliance for which the flamboyant prince would pay heavily in future.

Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge used Sihanouk as a figurehead in the civil war which ended with their takeover in April 1975. They then held him prisoner in his own palace while they conducted a systematic reign of terror lasting almost four years.

Though he had vowed never again to be king, Sihanouk was chosen head of state after a 1991 U.N.-brokered peace treaty officially ended the conflict. In September 1993 he reclaimed the crown as a symbol of national reconciliation and unity.
